lead: Paul at Corinth is told in a vision not to be afraid, and he stays a year and a half. When a case is brought against him, the Roman governor refuses to hear it, and the word goes on. In the Gospel Jesus tells the disciples that their sorrow will be like the pain of a woman in labour: real, but turned into a joy that no one can take away. Psalm 47 sings of God, king of all the earth, the Lord whose kingdom the apostle is carrying into the cities of Greece.

r.h: Do not be afraid, but speak
set: Paul came to Corinth after Athens (18:1). He found work and lodging with Aquila and Priscilla, Jews lately expelled from Rome by the emperor Claudius, who were tentmakers like himself (18:2–3). When many in the synagogue would not accept his message, he moved next door to the house of Titius Justus. Crispus, the official of the synagogue, believed with all his household (18:4–8). Corinth was a large, rich port city, the capital of the Roman province of Achaia.

Background. An inscription found at Delphi, a letter of the emperor Claudius, names Gallio as proconsul of Achaia. From it scholars date his term to about AD 51–52, and this gives one of the surest dates in the life of Paul. Gallio was the brother of the philosopher Seneca.
str: vv. 9–11: the vision at night, and Paul stays a year and six months.
vv. 12–13: some opponents bring Paul before Gallio’s tribunal.
vv. 14–16: Gallio refuses to judge a dispute about their own law.
v. 17: Sosthenes is beaten, and Gallio takes no notice.
v. 18: Paul sails for Syria with Priscilla and Aquila; the vow at Cenchreae.
kw: The word spoken to Abraham, to Mary, to the shepherds, and now to Paul. It is not a promise that nothing will hurt; it is a promise of presence: “for I am with you”.

The governor of a senatorial province such as Achaia. Luke uses the exact title, as he does for Sergius Paulus in Cyprus (13:7). Such accurate titles are one reason historians take Luke’s account seriously.

The raised platform from which a Roman magistrate gave judgment. A large stone platform of this kind still stands in the forum of ancient Corinth. Paul later wrote to the Corinthians that all of us must appear before the judgment seat (bēma) of Christ (2 Corinthians 5:10).
vv: “Do not be afraid, but speak and do not be silent;
Paul had arrived in Corinth, as he says himself, “in weakness and in fear and in much trembling” (1 Corinthians 2:3). The Lord meets the fear of the preacher at night, before it can silence him.
for there are many in this city who are my people.
The Lord already counts as his own people many in Corinth who have not yet heard the Gospel. The missionary does not bring God to a city; he finds God already at work there.
see to it yourselves; I do not wish to be a judge of these matters.

Luke means a particular group of opponents in Corinth, not the Jewish people, and the synagogue official Crispus had already believed (18:8). Gallio sees only a quarrel about words and names. His indifference becomes a protection: for the time being, Roman law will not forbid the preaching.
At Cenchreae he had his hair cut, for he was under a vow.

Cenchreae was the eastern port of Corinth (Phoebe was a minister (diakonos) of its church, Romans 16:1). The vow was probably a private vow of thanksgiving of the Nazirite kind (Numbers 6). Paul the apostle of the Gentiles still keeps the devout practices of his own people.
ch: The Church has always read the vision at Corinth as a word to every preacher and catechist: fear is not a reason to be silent, because the Lord is with those he sends. The same promise closes Matthew’s Gospel: “I am with you always” (Matthew 28:20). Paul’s long stay at Corinth gave rise to two of his greatest letters, 1 and 2 Corinthians. The names in this chapter, Priscilla, Aquila, Crispus and perhaps Sosthenes, who is named with Paul at the start of 1 Corinthians, remind us that the Gospel was carried by households and friendships, not by one man alone.

r.h: Your pain will turn into joy
set: We are at the Last Supper, near the end of the farewell discourse. Jesus has just said, “A little while, and you will no longer see me, and again a little while, and you will see me” (16:16), and the disciples do not understand. He answers with a picture every family knows: a woman in labour.
str: v. 20: you will weep, the world will rejoice; your pain will turn into joy.
v. 21: the woman in labour and the joy of the child born.
v. 22: “I will see you again”, and a joy no one will take away.
v. 23: on that day you will ask nothing of me; the Father will give in my name.
kw: The same word for the disciples’ grief and the mother’s pain. The sorrow is not denied or hurried over. It is turned, the very same sorrow, into joy.
In John “the hour” is the hour of Jesus’ Passion and glory (2:4; 12:23; 13:1). Here the mother has her hour too: the Cross is pictured as a birth.
Jesus’ joy runs through the discourse: “so that my joy may be in you, and that your joy may be complete” (15:11). It does not depend on what the world gives or takes.
vv: you will have pain, but your pain will turn into joy.
Jesus does not say that joy will replace the pain, as if it were simply forgotten. The pain itself will be changed, as Good Friday becomes the way to Easter.
When a woman is in labor, she has pain, because her hour has come.

The prophets used the same picture for the coming of God’s new age: Zion in labour giving birth to a new people (Isaiah 26:17–19; 66:7–14). Many Christian readers have also seen here the Church, and Mary at the foot of the Cross, becoming mother in sorrow.
and no one will take your joy from you.
Easter joy is not a mood. It rests on a fact: “I will see you again”. What rests on the Risen Lord cannot be taken by any persecutor or loss.
ch: The Church reads this Gospel in the Easter season because it explains the Easter experience from the inside: the disciples’ grief on Good Friday and their joy on Easter morning (20:20). The Second Vatican Council opens its constitution on the Church in the modern world with the words “the joys and the hopes, the griefs and the anxieties” of the people of this age, which are also those of the followers of Christ (Gaudium et Spes 1). Christian joy does not ignore sorrow; it carries it to the Lord, who turns it.

qa: Does Christian joy mean we should not grieve?

No. Jesus says plainly, “you will weep and mourn”. He wept himself at the tomb of Lazarus (11:35). The promise is not that we will never grieve, but that our grief is not the end. It will be turned into a joy that no one can take.
study: What fear keeps me silent when I should speak of my faith? What does the Lord’s “I am with you” change?
Which sorrow in my life am I being asked to give to the Lord, so that he may turn it into joy?
